summary: Argues that mail senders should be able to assign a priority to messages, as suggested in RFC 539. It answers an objection in RFC 555 that urgency levels need defined effects on the mail server, noting that people, not programs, will usually pick the priority and may do so inconsistently.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 577 argues that a mail message should be able to carry its sender's view of its urgency. It suggests interpretations for values from 0 to 10 but leaves recipients and server processes to decide what to do with them.

subtitle: An argument for carrying sender-assigned urgency in mail.

tldr.problem: The RFC discusses whether mail should carry urgency information even though people may assign priorities inconsistently.
tldr.mechanism: The author proposes carrying a priority value as information, leaving human recipients and mail-server processes to decide how to act on it.
tldr.outcome: The RFC suggests meanings for selected values on a scale from 0 to 10, including example guidance for automated mail.

facts.label: Value 10
facts.value: Phone in the middle of the night, if necessary

today: RFC 577 is an argument about how mail protocols might carry priority information, not a complete specification of server behavior.

sections.title: Priority as Information
sections.content:
RFC 539 proposed letting mail senders assign a degree of priority. RFC 555 objected that the effects of urgency on the mail server had not been defined. RFC 577 responds that people, rather than automated systems, will usually assign priority and may do so inconsistently.

The author argues that urgency is still part of communication. The protocol should carry that information and let human recipients and server processes decide how to handle it, rather than require an automatic response for each value.
sections.plainLanguage: The author argues that mail should carry urgency information even if senders do not use it consistently. The receiver, not the protocol, can decide what action each value should trigger.

sections.title: Suggested Urgency Values
sections.content: The RFC suggests values from 0 through 10 and gives example meanings for some of them. A value of 10 could justify a phone call in the middle of the night if necessary; 8 means delivery to the user's terminal now; 6 means delivery there only when the user is at the exec level; 4 means delivery after sign-on or before sign-off; 2 means standard-mailbox delivery; and 0 means junk mail. The author offers these interpretations to help programs that generate mail assign reasonable values.
sections.plainLanguage: The scale gives examples of how urgent different values might be, from ordinary mailbox delivery to immediate attention. These are suggested meanings, not automatic actions required of every mail server.

sections.title: Who Decides What Happens
sections.content: The proposal separates the priority information from its handling. The sender supplies a value, but the RFC does not define a fixed server action for every level. Human recipients and server processes may decide together how to respond to the information.
sections.plainLanguage: A priority value tells the receiver what the sender thinks, but does not force a particular delivery action. People and mail programs can use the information as they choose.
